section_1.title: Introduction: The Digital Ledger
section_1.content: Define the problem of 'Double Spending' in digital currency and introduce the ledger as an immutable sequence of data blocks.
section_1.example: Imagine a digital 'magic notebook' where Alice gives Bob a token; everyone in the room must agree that Alice had the token before the transaction is recorded.

section_2.title: The Hash Function: The Digital Fingerprint
section_2.content: Explain SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm). Focus on the 'one-way' property: it is easy to compute a fingerprint from data, but impossible to recreate data from the fingerprint.
section_2.example: Visual: A blender turning a bowl of fruit (data) into a smoothie (hash). You can't turn the smoothie back into the original fruit.

section_3.title: Proof of Work: The Mathematical Puzzle
section_3.content: Introduce 'Mining' as finding a 'nonce' (number used once) that, when combined with transaction data, results in a hash starting with a specific number of zeros. This requires immense computational trial-and-error.
section_3.example: Visual: A digital lottery where 1,000 robots are trying to guess a 6-digit combination. The first one to guess it gets to write the next page in the ledger.

section_4.title: Public-Key Cryptography: Digital Signatures
section_4.content: Prerequisite: Modulo arithmetic. Explain how users prove ownership using a Private Key (a secret number) and a Public Key (a derived coordinate on an Elliptic Curve).
section_4.example: Visual: A 'lock and key' animation where Alice uses her private key to sign a transaction, and the network uses her public key to verify it without ever seeing the secret private key.

section_5.title: Synthesis: Chain Integrity
section_5.content: Explain how each block contains the hash of the previous block, creating an unbreakable chain. Changing one digit in block 1 changes its hash, breaking the link to all subsequent blocks.
section_5.example: Visual: A row of falling dominoes. Each domino is etched with the 'fingerprint' of the one before it. If you move one, the whole sequence collapses and alerts the network.

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
